Thanks everyone for your viewpoints.  I know the developers are keeping an eye on these topics and weighing all opinions in order to try to satisfy as many people as possible.

twoeyedjack: That index card thing is fascinating, as it fundamenally changes the way players will look at things.  It's actually an extremely "crunchy" solution, the sort of thing I've only ever seen before in video games (which have very rigid success criteria and literally zero room for improvisation regarding them).  If the GM writes "Convince Haka to stand down" on an index card, attacking her isn't even going to occur to them, and they'd know instantly it would be a bad idea.  If an objective is named "Pile of Proletariats," they'll know they're done when there's just one Proletariat left (plus all the check boxes would be checked).  Similarly, when I saw the "Locating and saving Argent Adept" in the book, I wondered whether that would even occur to players on their own (and in the Play Better podcast, it did not), but if you write it down and show it to them, then they know.

I agree with Spiff: the topic of index cards and their effect on gameplay totally deserves its own topic.  Using them eliminates a lot of my concerns, but at the cost of verisimilitude.

PlatinumWarlock: I dunno.  Clearly the core rulebook is incomplete, although I anticipate that it's only missing the creation rules, setting information, and the like.  I expect all the gameplay rules are there (minus the stuff they play forgot to write down).

However, the adventure modules should be complete.  To take scaling as an example, clearly they had some idea that scaling needed to take place.  Issue #1 is perfectly adequately scaled, since it's nearly all minions and each group has one minion per hero.  I would probably take an extra step and scale the lieutenant down to a starting d8 for two or three heroes, and maybe to a d12 for six heroes, but it's close enough.  But the later adventures, #6 in particular, don't scale very much at all.  Even if the core rulebook has a section on how to build combat encounters to be an appropriate challenge for the number of heroes, for a GM to make use of that when playing a module, they'd have to use those rules to reverse-engineer the existing encounters, figure out how many heroes they were designed for, and then add, subtract, strengthen, or weaken the enemies (or add or remove required Overcomes) to re-scale them.  That's a whole lot of work (which needs to be done in preparation, not at the table) when the module could have simply said that Baron Blade's HP = 30 + 10/hero, for instance.

Agreed; there seem to be simple solutions which could aid with the scaling which probably should have been included.

I can't help but note that the three adventures that seem to be the best put-togther (1, 2, and 6) are written by Christopher and Philippe, while the three that seem to have bigger issues in scaling, coherency, and overall formatting (3, 4, and 5) are written by Christopher and Clark.  Perhaps there's a "same page" issue between Phillipe and Clark that needs to be ironed out, possibly within the context of "Here's how we choose whose stats to present" and "Here's what we do to scale encounters, based on player count."

twoeyedjack:

I'm already more on the Jeysie side of things as far as looking for a more narrative driven system, and I'm super excited about the Sentinels RPG system since it runs so well.

While I appreciate the narrative stuff tons, my love is particularly for a system that will break far less when any of the lovable loons in my group do something unexpected, with that being a nice side effect of the more narrative approach.

Like to give an example: One of the most memorable moments in my d20 group was when one of the players decided they were going to push a couple crates of bottles of soda onto an enemy below. It took the poor DM literally a good half-hour of combing through various d20 rulebooks to try to figure out how to adjudicate it, including some of us helpfully looking up how much a couple crates of soda should weigh.

But in contrast, in this system, near as I can tell, you could pretty much handle that as a risky action, with it taking about a couple minutes to throw together the appropriate three dice, and then I'm wagering it probably would take much less than another 28 minutes to come up with a reasonable narration and minor twist.

That's why I felt a little put out when people accused me of being elitist in saying stuff seemed easier to figure out here, when my metric for saying stuff seems easier was looking back at particularly gameplay-halting things my group's players did in d20, and then looking them up in this system to see how this one compares. And generally my perception was "It would be way less of a PITA here, at the price of having to put a little more work into coming up with narrative stuff."

And as someone whose sense of direction is abysmal at best, I appreciate that the combat seems to be far less reliant on precise position, as opposed to my days of old staring forlornly at the GameTable map on the screen in confusion and finally saying "guys I give up, can someone just tell me what direction I should go in to attack whatever annoying orc lackey is the closest to being dead"?

posts.cooked: I'm not convinced that the scaling is as necessary as some in this thread.  All the adventure modules from my youth said right up front something like, "for 3-4 characters levels 8-10".  As long as it's stated on the cover how many characters the adventure is designed for then bringing fewer or more than that is on the gamers, not the adventure writer.  If that kind of guidance isn't given so that the players can't know how many characters is the "right" number of characters, then I would agree scaling becomes necessary.

Well, now that that's out of the way, all I have to offer (of value) is that, as an experienced role-player, the game took some getting used to during the Gen Con demo. Note cards may have helped, but would have also done too much of the work for us...perhaps. As an experienced GM, though, running the game was very difficult when compared to how much - and this is the important part - a concrete structure of rules assisted me by way of holding my hand.

I'm a creative player. I'm a creative GM. My creativity, though, has never been a necessary tool in the game, but always a flavorful addition to it. Now, my experience is more limited to games like D&D and Pathfinder, but FATE has always caught my attention. Necessitating adaptability and creativity does add a new set of difficulties to GMs unused to running such games - at least it did for me. Without a structure that let me know I was doing everything the 'right' way, it felt like I was doing everything the 'wrong' way, when most of Sentinels gears around doing things 'any*' way. It takes some getting used to. 

As a longtime player of Mutants and Masterminds, I was looking forward to something more along those lines, just stylized for SotM.

I didn't get what I was looking forward to. I got something different, something outside of my comfort zone.

Sometime I'm excited to get the hang of.

I think both Mindwanderer and Jeysie have valid points that they each obviously feel very strongly about. Twoeyedjack and others lent some excellent perspective to all of this, too. I'd like to see these cracks, chips, and smears we see get patched and polished by the time the core rulebook comes out, but that isn't going to happen unless we're constantly reminding ourselves to give constructive feedback. It doesn't always have to be positive, mind you. There's value in negati...wait. That doesn't make sense. Anyway, you get what I'm saying. If you have a criticism, present it with solutions. If you have compliments, reinforce the fundamentals of the game that you feel are responsible for them.

God, that sounds so lecture-y. Anywho, this is a solid online community that I'm relatively new to, and I hate to see disagreement turn to disrespect. So let's like...be excellent to each other and stuff.

posts.name: The Blue-Eyed Bard
posts.cooked:
"Fun" can be tricky sometimes, though. Are the players having more fun if they have to figure everything out, or if they're given notecards plainly spelling out their objectives? Is taking a wild guess only to have it fail still fun because we got to take the guess? If there a thousand ways to get from Point A to Point B, but no actual road connecting the two, are you ever sure you're headed in the right direction? And, more importantly, does it matter if you are?

I've never been much for modules - they've always been too linear and confining for my tastes. It feels - to me - that these modules are the opposite, especially if they are meant to serve as a learning tool for new GMs. I struggled with inventive, relevant twists, myself. And yes, the Gameplay Guide does lay out all the nuts and bolts of the game, but, well...I want to know what colors this ride can come in, y'know? I love coming up with all my own stuff, but I also like being nudged into directions I might not have thought of on my own.

Regardless, I don't think anyone meant to go into this discussion with both barrels blazing. If you lot are anything like me, you occasionally find yourselves lacking in social graces and charm and - especially if you're anything like me - hypersensitive to criticisms of your perspectives and values.

All I really find helps then is to remind myself that there are two kinds of people I come across throughout the day: People who aren't douchebags and people who don't matter. Any confusion between one and the other is usually on me.

My view is that in the end any twist is fine so long as it keeping things moving. Even well-worn cliches can be fun in the right context, particularly in a lighthearted comic book inspired RPG. Why worry?

Honestly, as someone used to a group where people played literal ninja secretaries and ventriloquist bards as PCs, where toilet paper and action figures were viewed as useful inventory items, where conversations like "Can the computer scan for dead lifeforms?" "That's an oxymoron." "Dead deadforms, then?" "No, that requires the optional deadform scanning module."  cropped up regularly, and where whenever the GM asked "what option do you want to take" the answer was invariably "whatever leads to the funniest result", I feel like worrying too much about being perfect with your creativity is a bit overrated.

My view pretty much is: So long as you put in whatever effort you can, I'll do my best to help you make it work. I prize earnestness and sincerity over being perfect.

Hi Gang!  I am not sure if some of these questions got answered and I have the same ones.  I have a LOT of experience running superhero campaigns using other systems and a fair amount with Powered By The Apoc (PBtA) games and I have questions.  Here are the initial bullets with my comments.  My comments start with [John].

  • Harvester Spider Bots can't reach heroes to attack them if said heroes are flying.  But the spiders shoot laser beams from their eyes, so why not?  [John] Sure they can shoot them at range.  Very free form.  :)
  • "Avoiding Collateral Damage" in issue 2 introduces a new concept: twists that get dramatically more severe as the scene tracker progresses.  Nothing in the core rules suggest this should happen.  I see some later scenes apply the same concept.  This seems unbalanced--the GM would be acting strongly in the players' favor if they used scene twists when in the green and "general" twists while in the red, and vice-versa.  I'm not sure how to choose twists in a way that's fair, consistent, and interesting.  [John] TOTALLY AGREE!  With PBtA the difficulty of the twists stays the same.  This is the first time I have seen a concept of increasing the difficulty of these.  With the PC is is COOL and makes sense.  When the pressure is on the heroes step up.  I am not getting...when the pressure is on the environment gets more inherently dangerous???
  • There's basically no information on the poor family that lives in this house.  I assume the GM makes it up as needed, but I don't know why they should--this info could easily have been in the book.  [John] Too funny.  Agree.
  • The VoidHeart has one special ability it can use instead of a basic action: create a dark hero and simultaneously advance the scene tracker.  Under "tactics," however, the book says that an Overcome can be used to disable "one of the VoidHeart's special actions".  Does this disable one aspect of its one special action (the manifestation or the advancement) or is that a mistake?  [John] Confused too.  Clarification anyone?

  • Harvester Spider Bots can still shoot webs at flying heroes and bring them down that way, or just have more spider bots focusing on the people on the ground.

Reading over the thread, my general response (which I think echoed some earlier comments) is that:

Sentinels RPG (SRPG) is kinda crunchy, but not really. It requires perhaps more work than D&D. D&D has a stat or rule for practically everything. Want to pick a lock? You got a Lockpicking skill. Anyone who wants to pick a lock either uses Lockpicking or does it unskilled. If your characters wants to pick a lock, they go to the Lockpicking section.The rules tell the GM how a character can pick a lock.

SRPG is a bit more freeform. Someone playing Wraith might decide: "Use Agility + Investigation" because you're trying to Investigate what's on the other side of the lock, and I don't understand the difference between Dexterity and Agility." :) Or "When I selected Agility, I intended it to mean Dexterity, too."

Someone else running Wraith might say "Use Gadgets + Stealth", because you're using a lockpick and you're trying to sneak through the complex by getting past the door.

And someone who is a number cruncher might say, "I'm going to use Throwing Knives + Investigation, because I've got d10s in both and those are my highest dice. Justification? I'm using a throwing knife to pick the lock."

That's not unique: some of the Cortex RPGs do the same thing. But I can see why it's kinda... schizophrenic. It often requires a combination of thinking outside the box/creativity, and number crunching. And sometimes it gets down to personalities and approaches: what if the GM thinks that using a throwing knife to pick a lock is nonsense? What is the person who chose Wraith (or built their own character) because they wanted to pick locks and thought it was a good combo to do so disagrees with the GM? Let's say that both sides honestly believe their points of view: you get some bad feelings.

You also get some players who do try to number crunch/game like that. Or are they? They rarely say that they do, and often they don't think that they are. Or they think that it's all a part of that type of RPG. Or maybe it's how they get their kicks. Externally, how do you tell the difference between the different types? Is there a difference? Is one "better" than the others?

And yes, this kind of thing should theoretically be run up with the GM before character selection/design. But... there's a lot of potential situations, and several players.

How does this all tie in to the discussion? It seems like we have two sides, one taking the Type A GM and the hardcore approach (which isn't unique to D&D, and D&D-ish GMs), and the other taking the Type B GM and the "If you think of it, they will come and I will approve" approach. The starter adventures seem to be written the same way, IMO. Some parts are very "Do what you will" and some parts are "Here are very specific guidelines and rules for dealing with these situations."

Just my two cents.

Having finished Issue 1 in the PBP as Unity, I have some more feedback to add.

Regarding the issue:

It runs pretty smoothly, but the "Horde of Harvesters" is a bit wonky.  First, the players need to realize that unlike all the other spiders, you don't just hit the horde with damage, you use an Overcome to neutralize all of them at once.  It's unclear why they can't just do the same thing to kill all the other spiders without using an area attack that's actually on their character sheets.

Second, the swarm of spider-bots is described as being unstoppable because they're being replaced so quickly, yet the mothership only lays up to 5 new spiders a round.  It doesn't really state in the issue that the mothership is in fact laying way more than that, but the others are going to the tree.  Without that, it's hard to realize that destroying the mothership means that Overcome actions can be used to clear the tree.

Both problems are solved by using index cards with checkboxes for objectives, as described above.  Once again, it really seems that this was the intended method of playing the game despite not being overtly stated in the books.

Regarding Unity:

Unity... has some problems, I feel.  She's fun but she has some design flaws.

  1. She's far too dependent on minions.  I get that it's her whole archetype, but the minions are fragile and it's easy to find yourself without any, either because they were destroyed or because it's a new scene.  At the beginning of an adventure, it's fine, she just makes them.  But when she reaches Yellow status, if she doesn't have any minions, she has to choose between falling back to a Green ability or using Brainstorm.  I ended up using Brainstorm a lot; it's a great move even though it keys off a d6 power.  But if you're using that, you're ignoring Unity's archetype and over half her ability set.  When she reaches Red, she can start making two minions a round, but at that point the scene is almost over and the time to build up your forces is past.  Usually only rounds 7 and 8 are Red, and if she makes minions in round 7 they'll only get one chance to act.
  2. Her Principles are unbalanced.  Every single one of her Powers is technology-related.  Other heroes are more diverse and can approach challenges in different ways.  With Unity it's technology or bust.  This means that she's going to be using Principle of the Gearhead virtually constantly.  Principle of Levity, on the other hand, is extremely challenging to use, and even if she can think of a way to use Levity with one of her Powers, she could probably have used Gearhead too!  If she had Banter or Insight as a Power (several other heroes have Insight as a Power), it would help a ton.
  3. She has both Science and Technology as Qualities.  That seems redundant, and since Technology uses a bigger die, she'll be using that pretty much exclusively.  And again, since all of her Powers are technology-related, using that big d10 Technology die is going to be the "correct" choice nearly every time.  I ended up using Former Intern and Insight just for fun a few times, but I could have easily justified Technology instead every time.
  4. Overcome is a trap choice for minions.  As Dave described, the success table for Overcome is designed with Principles in mind.  Mostly the heroes will be using their Principles when Overcoming, and as a result they'll usually either succeed outright or succeed with a minor twist.  Minions, on the other hand, usually have a d8 to roll at best, meaning the chance of outright success is only 1/8.  They're much more likely to create twists or fail, and you do not want a bunch of minions creating additional twists.  Twists are serious business, even minor ones, and unless those twists are directed solely back at the minion that created them, they can get the whole team into a lot of trouble very quickly.  And if you're using an action to create a minion that acts once, creates a twist, and then either destroys or hinders itself, Unity would have been better off just taking that Overcome action herself.  If you want minions to help with an Overcome situation, give them the Boost action.

3/8 chance of getting a success with a twist is not bad. They rolled and got a good number. It was a free action for Unity (she gave a persistent boost) so she was free to help the fight. Really?  My read of the minor twists is that they're really bad, for the most part.  "Take damage equal to the max die" will either destroy the bot outright or weaken it permanently.  "Hindered using Max + Min" doesn't really apply to one die, but it should be about enough to guarantee the bot's next attempt is a failure (or is destroyed on its next save).  The scene escalating would be disastrous.  Being separated from the rest of the group is situational, but presumably without guidance from Unity it would stop being useful.  Summoning another enemy minion could be bad or not depending on turn order and whether the other heroes have mass attacks.  And story-based twists waste the other heroes' time, which also makes the effort a net loss.

Hasty Augmentation is an interesting choice for a minion.  I was about to say I wouldn't use it, since then you've used two turns on something that can be destroyed instantly, but then it occurred to me that a persistent boost can be used on minion saves as well!  That's actually not a bad move, depending on the enemy.  And if the bots survives until Unity or the scene reaches Yellow, she can heal it using Flash Forge, and as near as I can tell it would keep the Augmentation.
